Call centers: 38% of agents aren't satisfied with their job

A lot is said about customer experience, much less about the experience of the people who deliver it. Yet in a call center, the quality of a conversation depends heavily on the state of mind of the agent who picks up. An exhausted or unmotivated agent cannot deliver a remarkable experience, even with the best script in the world.

A 2017 survey in the United States by Aspect and Conversion Research, published by Statista, measured how satisfied customer service agents were with their job. The results are old, and we present them as such, but they remain a useful benchmark for a job whose broad conditions have changed little.

What the 2017 survey said

62% of agents surveyed said they were satisfied with their call center job. In other words, 38%, almost four in ten, were not. The gap between men and women was marked: 70% of men said they were satisfied, compared with 61% of women.

These figures do not tell the whole story of the job, and they date from 2017. But they show that a significant share of the people who answer customers every day do not find their work satisfying. For a role in direct contact with customers, that is not a detail.

They also raise the question of what weighs most on these agents: workload, repetition, the tension of some conversations, or a lack of recognition.

A shrinking workforce

Statista's dossier on call centers in the US adds another angle. The number of customer service representatives peaked at about 2.92 million in 2019, then gradually declined. In 2025, there were about 2.6 million.

Fewer agents does not mean fewer customers to serve. Contact volumes remain high, and some simple requests are now handled by automated tools. Agents therefore increasingly focus on complex or tense situations, the ones that require listening and judgment.

That shift makes their work more emotionally demanding, and the question of their satisfaction even more important.

Agent experience and customer experience are linked

A satisfied agent listens better, gets more involved and finds solutions more easily. An agent who endures their job answers mechanically, cuts conversations short and unwittingly passes their weariness on to the customer. Customers notice, even over the phone.

The causes of agent dissatisfaction are often the same as those of customers: recurring problems that never get fixed, calls where the agent has to absorb a customer's anger without being able to act on the cause, procedures that force them to repeat the same explanations.

Improving one improves the other. Reducing repetitive reasons for calling relieves both the customer and the agent.

This is also why turnover in call centers is such a costly issue. Every agent who leaves takes experience with them, and every new agent needs time before handling difficult conversations with confidence.

Understanding conversations to help agents

Automatic language analysis can play a useful role here, provided it is used to understand rather than to monitor. By reading every transcribed call, it identifies the reasons for contact that come up most, those that generate the most tension, and those that could be solved upstream.

That information makes it possible to fix causes at the source: a poorly explained bill, missing information on the website, a delivery time that was badly communicated. Fewer difficult calls mean less pressure on teams. Our call centers page describes this approach.

The models used are Mistral, BERT, Llama, GPT or Claude depending on the case, and data stays hosted in France.

Spotting difficult calls

The analysis can also flag conversations that are especially charged with emotion. The goal is not to grade the agent, but to recognize that they have just been through a tough exchange, to offer recovery time or support, and to draw lessons for the team.

Managers who have that view can balance workload better, adapt training to real situations and recognize the work done on the hardest cases. It is a concrete lever to reduce the share of dissatisfied agents, and to improve the customer experience at the same time.

Finally, sharing positive customer feedback with agents matters as much as fixing problems. Knowing that a conversation really helped someone is one of the strongest sources of satisfaction in this job.
